item.title: ReactOS has spent decades trying to be a free Windows, so I ran my oldest apps on it
item.itunes:title: ReactOS has spent decades trying to be a free Windows, so I ran my oldest apps on it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever there's a paid version of a piece of software, naturally, there will be a handful of free alternatives that spawn to fill the user base that doesn't want to pay or pirate the premium option. Windows was no different, and even in 1996, when ReactOS was created, there were users that wanted an open-source, clean environment that they could trust with their applications and data.

ReactOS is a free, open-source operating system that was built to run Windows programs and drivers without any of Microsoft's own code. It's quite the reverse engineering effort, and the contributions date back to over 30 years ago, long before the advent of AI agents. It's still considered to be in an alpha state, but regardless, I gave it a test drive in a VM to see just how useable it is, and it surprised me in a lot of areas.

6 operating systems you can use entirely in your browser

You don't need to learn about VMs

3
By  João Carrasqueira

ReactOS and how it got here

It has been a long road

ReactOS was born out of FreeWin95, which was an attempt to build a free clone of Windows 95. That project largely got stuck in the planning phase and never released a build, but in 1998, developer Jason Filby took it over and renamed it to ReactOS. With this new name came a much more lofty goal, which was targeting Windows NT instead of 95, which became the foundation for every Windows version since.

Progress was very slow going at the start of the project, with version 0.1 of ReactOS arriving in 2003. You were able to boot from a CD but there was no GUI to speak of. Another flashpoint came in 2006, when there were growing concerns that some contributors to the project might've seen leaked Windows source code, which lead to a freeze and audit on the project. That slowed development down even more for a few years.

The jump to 0.4 in 2016 came with a much more Windows-like desktop, and releases have been dotted around since then. The latest version is 0.4.16, which is what I tested.

10 retro operating systems you can try out for a shot of nostalgia

Nothing ever truly dies on the internet and these retro operating systems are live and kicking and ready for you to use.

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Everyday stuff does work

Installation and normal apps are fine

I started by installing the 32-bit build of ReactOS in a VM on my home server, and after that went off without a hitch, I went straight to installing apps. I went for a web browser first, and while ReactOS does ship with one, I installed the latest version of Firefox posible, which is 52.9.0 ESR. This was the last release Mozilla shipped for Windows XP and Vista. It loaded firefox.com over HTTPS just fine, and it's only complaint was that the browser was out of date, but despite that, it rendered a pretty modern page cleanly enough.

Office-style work went just as well, as OpenOffice worked just fine, GIMP and Notepad++ were functional, and 7-Zip and WinRAR were also good, license nag and all. Even qBitttorrent connected to peer-discovery perfectly fine, too.

Using the Applications Manager meant I was getting the last version of each of these apps that actually supported Windows XP, which doesn't necessarily mean it's the original release from that era. It's a lot more practical for me to test these, as they have a much better chance of actually working over the original, worse behaved versions.

This 28-year-old open-source Windows alternative can finally run Half-Life 2

ReactOS is now capable of playing Valve's iconic first-person shooter.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Drivers run on ReactOS, too

Not just apps

This is where ReactOS really separates itself from something like Wine. Wine is a compatibility layer that alets Windows programs run on Linux and macOS, and ReactOS does borrow a lot of Wine's code, but the difference is it's a complete operating system that can load kernel drivers Windows uses.

CPU-Z is a prime example of this in action, because it needs a kernel driver. It's small, but it allows it to read processor details, which is something Wine couldn't do. On ReactOS the driver loaded, and CPU-Z reported the virtual CPU's clock speed and supported instruction sets. It got the processor's name wrong, but that's to be expected in a virtual environment like this.

This open-source Windows alternative finally gets a much-awaited speed boost

Faster networking is finally here

1
By  Rahul Naskar

It's still fragile underneath

They call it an alpha, and that's what you should expect

I ran into a lot of crashes and issues just installing certain applications, and that's not really a huge surprise since this is still an operating system in an alpha state.

The original release of .NET Framework 2.0, without the service pack, crashed the entire operating system. At the step where the installer starts "Installing native images," ReactOS hit a blue screen with a MEMORY_MANAGEMENT error. I rolled back and tried three more times, first with 2GB of RAM and then upping the VM to 4GB, to see if that might've been an issue, but it crashed at the same point every time.

Even when things did work, they sometimes still threw errors or crashed: Foxit Reader, which I used in place of Adobe Reader, blue-screened the system the first time it launched from the installer, but after a reset it launched normally.

Media playback was patchy. VLC played audio, but its default video output showed only a black window. MPC-HC wouldn't play anything, not a web stream and not even one of ReactOS's own startup sounds. I'm unsure if this is due to it running in a virtual environment or because of the OS itself, but I wasn't able to get it working regardless.

Running Windows apps on Linux just changed forever, and I was one of the first to try it

Things are diferent now

34
By  João Carrasqueira

It's far from a Windows replacement, but it's a neat project

ReactOS is far from being a daily-driver, but it's a fascinating effort to bring Windows functionality to something that is completely free and open-source. Even as a free, contained way to run XP-era software without a Windows license, it's far more capable than people might give it credit for.

item.title: The Acer Nitro V 16 gaming laptop with an RTX 5050 drops to just $1,099.99
item.itunes:title: The Acer Nitro V 16 gaming laptop with an RTX 5050 drops to just $1,099.99
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you've been shopping for a 16-inch gaming laptop this Black Friday, Acer has plenty of options. The Acer Nitro V 16 Gaming Laptop pairs an Intel Core 5 210H with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5050 Laptop GPU, and it's $1,099.99 on Amazon, down from its regular price of $1,349.99.

The Acer Nitro V 16 ANV16-I31-54PT is a 16-inch gaming laptop with an Intel Core i5-210H processor and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5050 GPU. It has a 1920 × 1200 IPS display with a 165Hz refresh rate and a 76Wh battery.

See at Amazon

Plenty to like at this price

RTX graphics and a 165Hz screen for fast-paced play

Acer says the Nitro V 16 is built for fast-paced gaming, and the parts list points the same way. You get an Intel Core 5 210H processor and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5050 Laptop GPU, with the processor handling general tasks and the GPU taking on game graphics. Acer says the combination delivers smooth visuals and responsive performance.

The screen is a 16-inch WUXGA panel with a 165Hz refresh rate. Higher refresh rates generally make fast motion look smoother, so it's the spec to watch if you play shooters or racing games. The 16-inch size is shared with the other Nitro V 16 models listed below, so the differences between them are mainly in CPU, GPU, and refresh rate.

The version we're featuring here is the Core 5 210H version, but Acer has pricier Nitro V models on sale. The ANV16-I31-73JB moves up to a Core 7 240H while keeping the RTX 5050 and 165Hz display, at $1,444.99 on Amazon. The ANV16-I31-97P6 steps up to an RTX 5060 and a 180Hz display at $1,869.99, and the ANV16-A31-R8XV pairs a Ryzen 9 270 with an RTX 5070, 16GB of DDR5 memory, and a 512GB Gen 4 SSD for $1,829.99. Measured against the $1,099.99 deal price, the Core 7 240H model costs $345 more for the same GPU and refresh rate; the RTX 5060 model costs $770 more; and the Ryzen 9 270 model costs $730 more.

If you'd rather go smaller, the Nitro V 15 (ANV15-A31-R514) has a 15.6-inch FHD IPS display with a 180Hz refresh rate, a Ryzen 7 processor, and an RTX 5060 GPU for $1,629.99. It's not cheap by any means, and if you want a higher-tier GPU, you'll have to spend more on one of these models. For most people who just want a 16-inch gaming laptop, though, the Core 5 210H is the one that keeps costs down.

The deal is part of Amazon's event, which began Nov. 19 and runs through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, though Acer notes limited availability and says offers can change without notice. At $1,099.99, a $250 savings from the $1,349.99 regular price and the lowest price we've seen on Amazon, it's an easy one to pick up. Grab the Acer Nitro V 16 on Amazon soon if you want it.

item.title: XNU Linux wants to run macOS apps on Linux by stuffing the entire macOS kernel into the system
item.itunes:title: XNU Linux wants to run macOS apps on Linux by stuffing the entire macOS kernel into the system
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • XNU Linux embeds Apple's XNU kernel into ARM64 Linux to run macOS apps natively, no hypervisor needed.
  • It booted macOS 27.2.1 on Ubuntu and runs macOS and Linux processes side-by-side on compatible ARM64 hardware.
  • It's experimental and requires ARM64 with PAC and 4K pages, specific hardware, and your own macOS copy.

The Linux community has made massive strides in getting Windows apps working on Linux, to the point where we can just run anything we want through Proton and see what happens.

But what if you wanted to use macOS apps instead? Well, instead of using virtual machines or reverse engineering, one project believes it has the solution: stick the entire macOS kernel into Linux and let it handle it all.

XNU Linux aims to bring macOS compatibility by using Apple's kernel

It's certainly an interesting way to solve the problem

Credit: Heyang Zhou

As spotted by Linuxiac, XNU Linux aims to make it easier to run macOS apps on your Linux machine. The best part is, it doesn't need to use any translation or hypervisor tech to achieve that goal; instead, it takes XNU, an open-source kernel for macOS from Apple, and stuffs it into an arm64 Linux kernel. This allows the macOS and Linux processes to run natively next to one another on the same CPU.

It seems to be making pretty big strides already; in fact, its creator, Heyang Zhou, claims they booted macOS 27.2.1 to the desktop using a stock Ubuntu install. You can check it out in the screenshot above.

The system requirements are pretty tight; it's only for ARM64 devices with Pointer Authentication (PAC) and 4K pages. It has only been tested on bare-metal Nvidia DGX Spark hardware and Apple Silicon Macs that are M1 or newer (running Linux inside a VM via krunkit or tart, though XNU still runs directly inside Linux without a second hypervisor), and you need your own copy of macOS.

If you'd still like to give it a try, head over to the XNU Linux GitHub page and download it from there. Just remember it's still an experiment, so be ready for any and all weirdness that arises when using new tech.

I built a Hackintosh via Proxmox on an SBC because — why not?

What could go wrong?

3
By  Ayush Pande

I attended Adobe MAX in Miami this year, and I wasn't exactly surprised to find that most of the announcements centered around AI. Sitting through the keynote, I could already anticipate the reactions I'd see the moment I opened social media, and I wasn't mistaken. Creatives and non-creatives alike shared the fear that Adobe was coming for human creativity.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've been covering the AI industry for years now, and I've watched this debate play out every time a new tool promises to make something that once required years of learning achievable in seconds. With AI now capable of handling everything from removing objects and changing backgrounds to editing entire videos, I went to MAX with one question in mind: Is there still a point in spending years learning tools like Photoshop when AI can do most of the work for you?

So, I decided to sit down with three senior Adobe executives and ask them exactly that. Their answers ended up being a lot more nuanced than just a simple yes or no.

The rise of AI editing had me questioning the need for traditional skills

Why spend years learning what AI can do in seconds?

There was once a time when learning Photoshop, Premiere Pro, or practically any professional editing software was a skill in itself. You'd spend months, if not years, learning your way around the interface, figuring out what each tool did, and mastering techniques that weren't exactly beginner-friendly.

I remember a time when people would turn to Facebook groups and Reddit communities asking experienced editors to remove unwanted people or objects from their vacation photos. And while removing a simple background was one thing, dealing with more complicated images, especially those involving shadows, reflections, or intricate details, required someone who actually knew their way around Photoshop.

I tried replacing Photoshop, Lightroom, and Acrobat with free vibe-coded alternatives, and they're surprisingly good

Got to give credit where credit's due

11
By  Mahnoor Faisal

A lot of Adobe's efforts over the last year, including what it announced at this year's MAX, have clearly been aimed at bringing more of that accessibility to traditionally complex creative tasks. From conversational editing to AI agents that can plan and execute entire workflows for you, Adobe is making it increasingly possible to create without necessarily knowing your way around its professional tools.

This is why I kept wondering where the need to learn your way around traditional editing tools like Photoshop even fits in anymore, especially when AI can already handle so much of the work for you. So, I figured, who better to ask than the very people working on these tools? I sat down with Zorana Gee, Senior Director of Adobe Creative Agents; Meg Donovan, Senior Director of Product Marketing for Creators and Generative AI; and Stephen Nielson, Senior Director of Product Management for Photoshop.

Zorana says AI can get you about 75% of the way there

The remaining 25% is where Photoshop comes in

When I asked Zorana Gee whether she thinks people still need to spend years learning traditional editing tools like Photoshop, she explained that AI can now get people a significant portion of the way toward their desired results, without requiring nearly as much technical knowledge.

She gave me an example of something she'd recently done herself. Zorana wanted to update her professional headshot to make it more fun and fitting for Adobe MAX 2026. Instead of opening Photoshop and manually editing the picture, she uploaded her existing headshot to Firefly, gave it the URL of the MAX website, and asked it to create something that incorporated the event's branding while keeping her appearance intact.

According to Zorana, the entire process took around 20 seconds. She estimated that achieving something similar manually in Photoshop could have taken even someone experienced with masking around two hours. And when she wanted more options, she simply asked Firefly to generate three more variations.

However, she doesn't think that means traditional editing skills are becoming completely irrelevant. She pointed out that while AI can get you perhaps 75% of the way toward your desired result, there's still a level of depth, precision, and control that tools like Photoshop have spent decades developing.

That's where she ultimately thinks the two approaches can complement each other. You can use AI to handle the bulk of the work, then turn to traditional editing techniques when you need to get the finer details exactly right. What was clear from her response was that she wasn't suggesting everyone needs to learn Photoshop or master traditional editing techniques.

Not everyone has the time to spend years learning their way around such complex tools, and AI is making it possible for those people to achieve results that would otherwise have been out of reach. But for those who do need that extra level of precision and control, knowing how to use these tools still has its advantages.

Meg says not knowing Photoshop doesn't make you any less creative

You don't need to master Photoshop to have good ideas

Meg Donovan had a slightly different take on the question. When I asked her whether learning traditional editing tools still matters, she told me that she actually hopes people, particularly creative professionals, continue learning the fundamentals.

Her reasoning made a lot of sense. Even if you're relying on AI to handle the actual editing, knowing the fundamentals helps you understand what you're trying to achieve in the first place. It also gives you an advantage when prompting AI tools, since someone who understands things like composition, lighting, and editing techniques can be much more specific about the results they're looking for.

Meg also pointed out that not everyone wants to learn how to edit, and that doesn't make them any less creative. She brought up an interesting statistic from Adobe's creator research, saying that around 34% of creators believe they've missed out on video jobs because they don't know how to edit. Yet, even among creators who do know how to edit, she said it's often one of the tasks they enjoy the least.

I switched from Photoshop to GIMP, but this free tool is better than both of them

GIMP was promising, until I started using this tool

7
By  Nolen Jonker

I could actually relate to this quite a bit. I'm a writer, and while I've been wanting to get more into video content creation, I simply haven't had the time to sit down and properly learn video editing. That doesn't necessarily mean I don't have ideas for the videos I want to create. It's just that turning those ideas into something I can actually publish has traditionally required a completely different skill set.

That's ultimately what I took away from Meg's response. Some people genuinely enjoy the editing process and want to master every aspect of it. Others might be better at coming up with ideas, storytelling, or other parts of the creative process, and would rather let AI take care of the technical work.

For Meg, the important distinction is that learning these skills can absolutely make you a better creative professional, but not knowing them shouldn't stop you from creating in the first place.

Stephen thinks there's only so much you can accomplish with a prompt

AI can make the edit, but can you make it yours?

Stephen Nielson, who leads product management for Photoshop, had an interesting perspective on this. When I asked him whether people still need to spend time learning Photoshop, his answer was that it really depends on the person and what they're trying to accomplish.

For some people, the editing process itself is what makes them feel creative. They enjoy getting hands-on with their work, experimenting with different techniques, and figuring things out themselves. For others, editing is simply something they need to get done, and if AI can handle it in seconds, why wouldn't they use it?

But Stephen brought up something I could relate to almost immediately. I've experimented with countless AI image editing tools, and one of my biggest frustrations is how often they fix one thing only to mess up something else. You ask an AI tool to remove an unwanted object, and it does exactly that, but suddenly your face looks different or some other detail in the image has changed. You then spend the next few prompts trying to fix everything it messed up along the way.

I replaced the Adobe suite with a free open source alternative that Claude can control directly

Artcraft clones Adobe's apps for free, and Claude can run them for you.

9
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Stephen acknowledged that this is a common problem with AI image editing, and it's precisely where he thinks Photoshop still has an advantage. During our conversation, he walked me through several of Photoshop's newer AI features, including Relight, Generative Restyle, and the upgraded Remove Tool.

With Relight, for example, you can add multiple light sources to an image, adjust their positions, change their colors, and control their intensity using interactive controls. You don't have to keep rewriting prompts and hoping the AI understands exactly what you're imagining.

He also demonstrated how Photoshop's layers and masks let you isolate certain parts of an image, so you can make changes without affecting everything else. When an AI-generated edit doesn't turn out quite right, you can manually fix the problematic areas without having to regenerate the entire image.

One thing Stephen said that stuck with me was that an interface can be worth a thousand words, if not more. And I think that sums up his argument pretty well. No matter how good AI gets at understanding natural language, there are certain creative decisions that are simply easier to make when you can see what you're doing and adjust things yourself.

Knowing Photoshop is still a skill worth having

What became extremely clear after chatting with multiple Adobe executives was that learning traditional editing skills isn't necessarily becoming irrelevant. It's just becoming less of a requirement, especially for people who simply want to get things done without spending years mastering complex software.

In a way, this reminds me a lot of what's happening with AI coding tools. You can now build entire websites and apps without knowing how to write a single line of code, but having a solid understanding of programming still gives you an advantage when something goes wrong, or you want more control over the final product.

I think the same applies to Photoshop. AI can handle a lot of the heavy lifting, and for the average person, that might be more than enough. However, for someone who wants to go beyond what AI produces and fine-tune every little detail, knowing how to use the tools yourself is still an incredibly valuable skill to have.

item.title: My old Android phone became my favorite PS2 handheld, and it only took one app
item.itunes:title: My old Android phone became my favorite PS2 handheld, and it only took one app
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Lately, I've been on a bit of a nostalgia trip. Specifically, I've been wanting to play some of my favorite PS2 games, and my old Android phone is the handheld I reach for. My days run long and busy, so I could never really justify the cost of a dedicated Windows handheld. But I have more than a few Android phones lying around that, when coupled with a telescopic controller, offer exactly the retro gaming experience I've been looking for.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Be it a quick round of Midnight Club 3 or a mission in Ace Combat, it's astonishing how far emulation on Android has come. NetherSX2 runs the games, and my telescopic controller gives me all the controls I need. It's a simple, cost-effective arrangement, but it's really all it takes to make the old phone feel useful again.

A telescopic controller makes PS2 games feel at home

Physical controls make racing and flying games easier

The base installation is easy enough. You'll want to install NetherSX2 from Github or the Play Store. Additionally, you'll need a PS2 BIOS file, which you can dump from your own console, but it's also freely available with a quick Google search. Next, of course, you'll need the game. Ideally, you'll want to rip the game to a compatible format from your own disc, unless you plan to sail the high seas. That's the gist of it.

While NetherSX2 offers plenty of ways to tweak the gameplay experience, things just work out of the box, and this is also where the telescopic controller comes in handy. The twitchy racing game truly benefits from your hand being able to quickly stretch out between steering, accelerating, and braking. And if you plan to make any progress in the title, playing via the touchscreen isn't going to cut it. In fact, I first tried it with just the touchscreen, and my thumbs covered enough of the picture that I ended up missing turns entirely.

With the phone clamped securely inside the controller, the screen sits in a comfortable position, and the controls are familiar enough to facilitate easy gameplay. Much better. The same goes for Ace Combat, but perhaps even more so. When you're tracking planes around you or maneuvering around incoming attacks, you want full access to all the controls. This time, including the thumbsticks. That won't happen via the touchscreen. The telescopic controller gives you all the controls you need to turn your phone into a dedicated handheld that fits perfectly.

The convenience of the telescopic controller is also why I prefer it. While practically any phone today is compatible with full-size gaming controllers, portability is part of the reason why I prefer this setup. My phone is obviously portable enough to slip into any pocket. The telescopic controller adds another dimension. Closed down, it fits into a jacket pocket or a small sling bag just fine, making the entire setup exceedingly portable.

Of course, the heavy lifting here is done by software. Specifically, NetherSX2 makes it exceptionally easy to get going once you've got everything set up. You don't need to browse folders, as it gives you a sufficiently serviceable list of titles that you can tap to play.

You also get quick save support, which is critical for on-the-go, start-and-stop play sessions. While all that is good, there are a few specific settings that I enjoy in the emulator. For example, you get both per-device and per-game settings. While the former is good for broader setup, like controller options and where to save states, the latter is handy for per-game fixes. If you're using an older phone for emulation, not every game is going to run perfectly from the get-go.

In this case, you can drop the rendering resolution to eke out a few more frames for a more consistent gaming experience. You can also adjust advanced filters to tweak the look and feel if you're running a more powerful phone. On my 2026 flagship, I'm getting consistent performance at 4x the resolution and could probably push it further still.

Elsewhere, there's support for patches, too. For example, there's a widescreen patch available for Midnight Club. This lets you fill out the frame on a modern widescreen phone, and the emulator can automatically apply these patches when available. That makes a big difference, as these patches are often critical to enabling the best possible performance, and you'll want to enable the auto-apply patches setting.

Beyond that, though, the experience is as easy as it gets with emulators. You'll probably want to keep an eye out for battery and thermal management on your phone. However, most mid-range and above phones these days are powerful enough that this isn't really a struggle anymore.

Giving my old Android phone a new life as a portable PS2

I've really come to enjoy this setup because it's given my old smartphone a job, and specifically a job that makes me come back to it daily. I'm enjoying the latest GTA, sure, but there's a wealth of old-school games still worth discovering from my childhood. And all it's taken is one app on my phone, a telescopic controller, and a game file to take that experience on the go at better-than-original resolution. Wild times we live in.

item.title: My local model isn’t as smart as Claude, but once I added these 4 features, I stopped caring
item.itunes:title: My local model isn’t as smart as Claude, but once I added these 4 features, I stopped caring
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every couple of weeks there's a new Claude model, and the distance between it and what I can fit on my 8GB card gets a little wider. A 9B model isn't going to reason like Opus, and even though the local model is capable, running it next to a Claude model highlights the gaps pretty quickly.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Raw intelligence isn't actually why most people open an AI app twenty times a day, though. Much of what makes Claude feel useful lives in the app around the model, and a local model sitting in a bare wrapper doesn't get any of those extras. Part of why local models can feel worse is probably because of this, but many of those missing pieces can actually be added to a local setup. And once I did, it didn't really matter that my local LLM isn't as smart as Claude.

A hotkey that brings my local model to whatever I'm doing

The quickest AI to reach is the one you use the most

Claude's desktop app has a feature called Quick Entry, which pulls up a small chat box over whichever app you're in with a keyboard shortcut. This is nothing new, many apps have a function like this, but it's not something you'll find in a local LLM or the majority of wrappers, including LM Studio.

What you need is a global hotkey, which is a shortcut an app registers with Windows so it works no matter what's open. This part has nothing to do with the model, since the app and Windows handle it, and the app has to stay running in the background to listen for the keys.

One of my favorite workspace apps to run my local LLM in is called Cherry Studio, and it has something called Quick Assistants which is the equivalent of Claude's Quick Entry. It's off by default, but once you turn it on then hitting Ctrl + E opens a little popup on top of whatever you're busy with, and I have mine pointed at an assistant that runs my local model. I also switched on the option to read my clipboard when it opens, which means whatever I've copied is already in a box with buttons to summarize, translate, or explain it.

I run OpenCode with a different model for every job, and I haven't hit a rate limit yet

I stopped leaning on one model for everything

By  Nolen Jonker

Web search so my local model can look things up

A small model doesn't need to know everything if it knows where to look

Every model basically stops learning on the day its training ended, so my local LLMs were never going to hold as much information as Claude models to begin with. Giving it web is pretty much the answer. When the model works out that it needs something current, it asks the app to run a search, and whatever comes back gets added to the chat for it to answer from. That only works with models that support tool calls, which the Qwen-based ones I use do.

There are different ways to get web search depending on how you run your model. My go-to is the Brave Search MCP in LM Studio, which requires an API key and editing LM Studio's mcp.json file, which is quite fiddly. Jan is the much simpler option because it ships with web search built in and lets you use it from the chat toolbar; it is on by default. And then Noema, which is my main mobile local LLM runner, also comes with its own search switch.

When Claude or ChatGPT searches for you, the whole conversation is on their servers, including anything you pasted in. Here, only the search query leaves my PC. That query still lands somewhere you don't control, for example, Brave keeps API query logs for up to 90 days for billing and troubleshooting, so it's not 100% private. But it is effective for armoring your model with more knowledge.

I run Claude, ChatGPT, and my local LLM through one interface, and I'm not going back

One window instead of three

1
By  Nolen Jonker

Giving it memory

So I can stop reintroducing myself or the project every time

Local runners don't necessarily carry personal memory between chats, and LM Studio doesn't have a built-in personal memory feature in my setup. My workaround was giving it access to a folder and asking it to save notes there, then pulling those files into the next chat. The way around this is an outside tool that has nothing to do with the model.

AnythingLLM is a great option because it has actual memory. It goes through your recent chats every few hours looking for facts about you and your work. Whatever it finds gets saved as short notes that show up in future chats. You can write your own as well, and keep each one tied to a single workspace or let it apply everywhere. Open WebUI and LibreChat also have memory features.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

19
By  Abhinav Raj

Picking one workspace app and sticking with it

Local LLM runners aren't built like Claude; you need a real workspace to replicate Claude

This is more of a tip than a feature, but if you want your local LLM to actually work like cloud chatbots, you need to pull it into an environment that has similar features. A runner like llama.cpp or LM Studio is built just to run models and expose controls you wouldn't find in cloud bots, but they don't really let you do anything beyond chat.

We all have that one feature that we can't do without, and for me that's Projects in Claude. Projects has a very specific user flow that's hard to replicate exactly, but you can get a version of it. This, once again, comes down to Cherry Studio for me. Its version of Project is called Assistants. Each assistant is a saved system prompt with its own model settings, and every chat you start inside it uses that same prompt and those settings.

It's not Claude Projects exactly, but it's close enough. If you have that one feature from a cloud AI app that you keep coming back to, look for an AI tool that has something similar. And I also recommend sticking with it rather than going on an endless hunt for the perfect replica, that way you can keep coming back to your work in the state you've left it instead of spreading your work across a million tools.

My local LLM can call Claude when it's stuck, and it changed everything about my local-first setup

Local LLMs aren't very good on their own

14
By  Anurag Singh

It's not about the model

I've been making do with running small models, and quite frankly, outdated ones at this point, because my card can't really handle more than that. And if this taught me anything, it's that the model and its benchmarks aren't all that important, it's more about the way you set it up and the third-party tools you use it with. Qwen 3.5 9B and Bonsai 27B are great, but they'd be useless to me if they can't use web or work in workspace tools.

item.title: My old Android phone runs a full Linux desktop with Termux:X11
item.itunes:title: My old Android phone runs a full Linux desktop with Termux:X11
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Self-hosting applications and building web servers to run and manage them gets quite interesting after some time. Earlier, my purview of a system was how powerful its hardware was. But now, I only think of one thing: “Can it be a server to run a couple of tools?” My curiosity led me down the dreaded path of Linux, an OS that I wouldn't have tried if it weren't for running and managing self-hosted tools. There are ample Linux distributions to keep you busy, and there's one for even the small-sized single-board computers like the Raspberry Pi.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

After successfully building servers out of old laptops, thin clients, and a couple of Raspberry Pi boards, my next target became old Android phones. I had moderate success with that endeavor. It made me question if a phone could actually run a Linux distribution with a desktop environment.

Not my first Linux encounter on Android

Termux is a familiar face

Termux is an application that can help you run a Linux-like command-line environment on your Android phone. It doesn't mess up your phone's OS or UI and lives separately, allowing you to conduct self-hosting experiments. There are other options such as Podroid as well, but it uses virtualization. You can imagine the subpar performance when you try to squeeze virtualization on something like a weak Android phone.

In Termux, I used the PRoot-Distro tool to install a Linux distribution and then add the packages I needed. The best part is that you can use the distro without rooting your phone, and that makes it a fun weekend project. Setting up something like Debian gives you access to a familiar package manager. I even set up a Jellyfin server that could serve my phone's media files on my local network.

I turned my old phone into a device that does something my $300 smart home gadgets can't

Turns out I haven't been utilizing my old phone enough.

1
By  Anurag Singh

But running a desktop environment wasn't on my list until a few weeks back. Since the phone could run a CLI OS without any major hiccups, the possibility of running a desktop environment seemed more exciting.

Termux:X11 gives you the desktop component

The combination makes it possible

For CLI distributions, you don't need anything except PRoot-Distro in Termux. But if you want to add a desktop environment to the existing distro and display it on your phone, you'll need Termux:X11. As the name suggests, it provides the X11 display server to view and interact with installed GUI apps. The actual desktop environment is installed in the Linux distribution, which is Debian in my case.

You start by installing two Android apps, both of which are available on GitHub and F-Droid. I had some issues installing Termux from GitHub, and Android threw a warning about the app being “suitable for very old versions.” So, I installed Termux using F-Droid just to get started, while Termux:X11's GitHub APK worked without problems.

A battered screen didn't stop me from turning my old Samsung phone into a functional home server

It's now an important part of my home lab

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Once you have them up and running, you need to add the x11 repo, the proot-distro tool for installing Linux distros, and the server executable for Termux:X11. You can use the following command:

pkg install x11-repo proot-distro termux-x11-nightly -y

Then, you can proceed to install a Linux distro of your choice with the PRoot-Distro tool. I picked Debian, but you have other options as well. The second command logs you in to the installed distro and shares a temporary directory between the distro and Termux:

proot-distro install debian
proot-distro login debian --shared-tmp

Thereafter, you need to install the XFCE desktop environment, its associated tools, a few necessary X11 packages, and your preferred GUI apps:

apt install sudo nano wget curl git dbus-x11 -y
apt install xfce4 xfce4-goodies -y
apt install x11-utils xauth -y
apt install firefox-esr gimp libreoffice -y

The last leg of this setup is to exit the current Debian session and start the X11 server. Then, launch the Termux:X11 app and switch back to the Termux terminal.

termux-x11 :0 &
proot-distro login debian --shared-tmp

Once you log in, all you need to do is set the display variable and launch XFCE. From there, you can launch individual apps in the terminal and then switch to the second app to view them. But I prefer launching them from the desktop.

export DISPLAY=:0
export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/tmp
dbus-launch --exit-with-session xfce4-session

Your mileage varies with the phone you choose for this experiment. I used my Samsung Galaxy S21 FE, a moderately powerful phone with 8GB of memory and ample storage to spare. On weaker, older phones, both the installation and the desktop environment’s responsiveness take a massive hit. In my case, the desktop environment loaded without any noticeable delays, but the app launches were noticeably slower.

Trying the Linux desktop on an Android phone

A mixed bag

I tested LibreOffice, GIMP, and Firefox for this experiment, and all of them worked decently after launch. Firefox loaded webpages without delays or broken elements, and GIMP could actually run without any errors. LibreOffice apps were also usable, and if you want to use them for typing or editing something, they won’t be a letdown.

The touchscreen interface takes a bit of time to get used to. Double-tapping on icons seems weird, and you’ll be better off with a keyboard and mouse connected to it via an OTG adapter with multiple ports. I built this setup using scrcpy, a tool that mirrors the phone screen on Windows, and it made typing long commands much easier. I highly suggest you use the tool and avoid the phone terminal for initial setup.

I tried turning my old Samsung Galaxy into a local LLM-hosting machine, and it worked better than I expected

I had to use several workarounds, though.

1
By  Shekhar Vaidya

While the apps run nicely, you might run into compatibility issues with them. Some features may also not work without further tweaks, like audio or video playback. Firefox could launch the YouTube interface, but it closed the server as soon as the playback started. It could be a memory issue or a permissions problem, but video playback always runs into issues. It worked after a few tries, but there were a lot of stutters at 1080p, and I didn't have the correct audio packages at that point.

Surprisingly good for an Android phone

Running a distro with a desktop environment inside an Android phone with its own OS overhead is baffling. The fact that the app works and can use the display server to run GUI apps is commendable. But you won’t find it as smooth as on a standard PC or SBC OS. It needs a lot of components to work and has to use resources left over after Android takes its share. Running this on a more powerful phone, with a bigger screen like a foldable, could be better for on-screen keyboard typing.

Termux

Termux is a terminal emulator app for Android OS.

Check Termux on Github

Double-tapping on icons seems weird, and you’ll be better off with a keyboard and mouse connected to it via an OTG adapter with multiple ports. I built this setup using scrcpy, a tool that mirrors the phone screen on Windows, and it made typing long commands much easier. I highly suggest you use the tool and avoid the phone terminal for initial setup.

I tried turning my old Samsung Galaxy into a local LLM-hosting machine, and it worked better than I expected

I had to use several workarounds, though.

While the apps run nicely, you might run into compatibility issues with them. Some features may also not work without further tweaks, like audio or video playback. Firefox could launch the YouTube interface, but it closed the server as soon as the playback started. It could be a memory issue or a permissions problem, but video playback always runs into issues. It worked after a few tries, but there were a lot of stutters at 1080p, and I didn't have the correct audio packages at that point.

Surprisingly good for an Android phone

Running a distro with a desktop environment inside an Android phone with its own OS overhead is baffling. The fact that the app works and can use the display server to run GUI apps is commendable. But you won’t find it as smooth as on a standard PC or SBC OS. It needs a lot of components to work and has to use resources left over after Android takes its share. Running this on a more powerful phone, with a bigger screen like a foldable, could be better for on-screen keyboard typing.

item.title: Anthropic’s new Claude Ship feature lets your assistant review, fix, and approve pull requests by itself
item.itunes:title: Anthropic’s new Claude Ship feature lets your assistant review, fix, and approve pull requests by itself
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Claude Ship gains two new features: PR Steward watches repos, fixes issues, and leaves comments.
  • Claude Approvals can automatically approve PRs, but managers can limit what it touches.
  • Available now to Claude Team/Enterprise users and works with GitHub repositories.

How do you feel about Claude checking out pull requests, working on them, and submitting fixes all by itself? I'd wager that people who use Claude to program would love the idea, but it would probably cause project maintainers to break into a cold sweat at just the thought of it.

Well, it appears that Anthropic thinks we're ready. The company is reportedly adding two features to Claude that take all the pesky human parts out of the pull request stage.

Anthropic adds PR Steward and Claude Approvals to Claude Ship

Whether or not that's a good thing is up to you

As reported by The Verge, Claude Ship is getting two new tools: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward stands by and keeps an eye out for any issues that appear within the repository. If it detects a problem, like a merge conflict, a failed CI check, or if someone (or something, like Code Review) gives negative feedback, it can deploy a fix and leave comments as to what it does.

Claude Approvals does pretty much what you'd expect it to do. If it sees a pull request and decides it fits company policy, it will automatically approve it. Fortunately, it seems Anthropic is giving project managers some control over what Claude can and cannot accept, so if you're worried about letting it loose on some really important parts of your project, you can keep it out.

You can give the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents a try in beta right now if you're a Claude Team or Enterprise customer, and it works with repositories on GitHub.

I asked Claude Code to build its own replacement, and it took just 15 minutes

15 minutes and one crazy idea later...

8
By  Mahnoor Faisal

item.title: This Samsung ultrawide monitor drops to just $854.98 for Black Friday
item.itunes:title: This Samsung ultrawide monitor drops to just $854.98 for Black Friday
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A browser, a spreadsheet, and a game running at once is a lot to ask of one standard monitor, and screen space is usually the first problem you run into. Samsung's 49-inch Odyssey OLED G9 (G93SC) gives you far more room to spread out, and for Black Friday it's $854.98 on Amazon, down from its $1,279.99 regular price.

The Samsung Odyssey OLED G9 (G93SC) is a 49-inch curved QD-OLED gaming monitor with a 32:9 Dual QHD (5,120 × 1,440) panel. It has a 240Hz refresh rate, a 0.03ms (GtG) response time, 1800R curvature, and DisplayHDR True Black 400 certification.

See at Amazon

You're getting a whole lot of screen for the money

A 49-inch OLED panel for work and play

The main draw is the 49-inch OLED panel in Samsung's Odyssey OLED G9 line. With that much display, you can keep a browser, a chat window, and a game open side by side, so one screen covers both work and downtime. If you're thinking about replacing a pair of monitors, you'd also get one continuous workspace instead of a bezel running down the middle.

This isn't a monitor for everyone. If you mostly use a screen for email and browsing, 49 inches is far more display than you need, and it'll take up a lot of desk space, so measure before you buy. It's also still a big-ticket purchase at this price, so it's worth considering if you truly want to go the ultrawide route. It's best for anyone who wants a single screen to replace a multi-monitor setup or to add extra room for games.

At $854.98 on Amazon, the 49-inch Odyssey OLED G9 is a good price if you have the desk space for it. If you've been eyeing a big OLED display, pick up the Odyssey OLED G9 soon, since prices tend to fluctuate.
